title: How to Learn Choreography Faster and Remember It
headline: How to learn choreography faster (and actually remember it)
h1: How to learn choreography faster and actually remember it
dek: Quick learners aren't magic. They map the piece, learn it in eight-counts, mark before they dance full out and check themselves on video. The method, step by step, with a 45-minute session plan.
description: How to learn choreography faster: map the piece, learn in eight-counts, mark it, use the mirror wisely, slow the video down, loop hard parts and film to check.

faq.q: How can I learn choreography faster?
faq.a: Watch the whole piece first to map its sections and repeats, then learn it one or two eight-counts at a time: feet first, then arms, then details. Mark each chunk before dancing it full out, say the counts aloud, chain new chunks onto old ones, slow the video down for hard parts and film yourself to check.

faq.q: How do dancers remember long routines?
faq.a: They lean on structure: named sections, repeated choruses, counts and musical landmarks such as a lyric that cues a move. Research on young ballet dancers found choreographed sequences are remembered far better than random ones, and that music helps recall. Regular review, a good night's sleep and starting runs from different sections all help too.

faq.q: Is marking choreography a good way to practise?
faq.a: Yes. Marking, dancing the choreography small with reduced movement, saves energy and seems to free attention for the order, timing and shapes. In a study of dance students, the routine practised by marking was performed better than the one practised full out. Mix marking with full-out runs.

faq.q: Should I mirror a dance video when learning it?
faq.a: Mirror it when the teacher in the video faces you, so their right is your right. If they face away from the camera, follow it as it is. Once you know a section, dance it facing away from any mirror and film it to check.

faq.q: What speed should I practise choreography at?
faq.a: Decode new moves at 0.25× to 0.5×, learn them at 0.5× to 0.75×, clean them at 0.75× to full speed, then perform from the top at 1×. Loop the one eight-count that keeps going wrong rather than running the whole piece again.
